To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

F1 killer cells with specificity for unusual antigens are generated in vivo when the parental stimulator cells bear both the target antigen and the F1 host antigen, and that the generation of these killer cells in vitro requires antigen on irradiated stimulator cells and the presence of F1 host antigen on the responding T cells.

potent lytic T cells can be generated in F1 animals with unusual antigenic specificities, and that these killer populations are generated in an in vivo primed state, and require an in vitro stimulation step.
F1 animals primed with parental target cells bearing unusual antigen systems and also having reactivity to host F1 alloantigens generate potent killer cell responses to those unusual antigens.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the generation of highly potent CTL responses to unusual antigens.

the generation of T cells with specificity for unusual antigens and with their potential for use as reagents for studying antigen recognition by T cells and for the development of novel immunotherapeutic approaches.
the generation of T cells with specificity for unusual antigens, such as alloantigens, and we are exploring the conditions under which this can be done in vivo.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

F1 animals primed with parental target cells bearing unusual antigens and possessing alloreactivity to F1 host antigenes can generate potent lytic T cells with reactivity against both the unusual and the alloantigens.

the killer cells described here are F1 antipaternal cytotoxic T lymphocyte populations generated in vivo and maintained in vitro by a combination of alloreactivity and the presence of antigen, and are capable of lysis of targets bearing the unusual antigens of either the parent strain.

the F1 antiparentral CTL responses described here require an in vivo primed, alloreactive, antigen-bearing population of cells that can be restimulated in vitro by antigen-bearing cells that lack the ability to stimulate the CTL in the absence of alloreactivity.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a single F1 animal can mount potent CTL responses to a large number of unusual antigens.

the generation of F1 antiparenal CTL with lytic specificity only to unusual antigens requires an in vivo sensitization with parental cells bearing both the relevant unusual antigens and alloantigens, and an in vitro restimulation with irradiated lymphoid cells expressing the unusual antigen.

the generation of these potent lytic F1 CTL populations requires an initial in vivo priming event, which is followed by an in vitro restimulation phase, and that both of these phases depend on the presence of antigen and alloreactivity on the same cell.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the F1 antiparenal system is a very useful model system for studying CTL responses to unusual antigens.

the F1 antiparentral CTL responses to unusual antigens, including MTA, are potent and readily induced, but require an in vivo primed condition in which the priming cell population bears the relevant target antigensis and has alloreactivity to F1 host cells.

the unusual antigens recognized by these killer cells, which are normally poorly immunogenic and not capable of generating effective helper responses in F1 hosts, can be presented in a way that is immunogenic for F1 T cells and leads to the generation of highly lytic CTL.
